title: The smallest version
hookLine: on bad days, do the one-breath version of everything

lines: UP AT THREE, CAR WON'T START.
FIVE MIGHT AS WELL BE FIFTY.
cards: Some days you'll do all five, and feel great. And some days the baby was up at three, the car won't start, your boss is angry, and someone you love is in the hospital. On those days, five practices might as well be fifty.
That's when a routine is in danger. Not on a good day. On a bad one, when the whole thing feels impossible, so you do none of it.
There's a way through, and it's almost embarrassingly small.

teach.b: The Stanford behavior researcher BJ Fogg has an example. If you want to start flossing, he suggests, begin by flossing one tooth. It sounds like a joke.

But one tooth is so easy you can't talk yourself out of it, and the habit, picking up the floss at the same moment every day, gets built anyway. On a good day, you'll do them all. On a bad day, one tooth still counts.
The Talmud has a saying, from a very different setting, that people often quote here: grasp too much, and you grasp nothing; grasp a little, and you've grasped something.
So shrink each of your five to its smallest version, the one-breath version. The breathing practice becomes one long exhale. The evening review becomes one question: what went well?
Gratitude becomes one good thing, said inside. The body scan becomes a single drop of the shoulders. The sunset becomes a glance at the window.
Service becomes one kind text. Each takes a few seconds. None is the full practice, and that's fine.
On bad days, the goal isn't growth.

It's continuity: keeping the thread unbroken, so it's there to pick up when the day gets better. There's something kind in this, too. A routine that only works on good days is really a reward for having good days.
A routine with a smallest version is there for you when you need it most.

how: Habit coaches often suggest a tiny fallback version of each habit, like one push-up or one line of a journal, for days when the full version won't happen.

o: the tiniest form of a practice, for the hardest days
a quick practice that replaces the full one for good
a breathing drill done once before every meal

games.q: each practice, shrunk — tap the pairs.

games.q: it's a terrible day. your five practices feel impossible. what do you do?
o: skip them all; try again when life calms down.
do the one-breath version of each.
force all five at full length.
games.why: the smallest version. on bad days, the goal is continuity, not growth.

practice: Take one slow breath in, and a long breath out; on a hard day, that's a whole practice. Then go through your five, one at a time, and find each one's one-breath version: on a bad day, this becomes that.
Rest in the breathing, and let the smallness feel like enough.

wordCard.voice: One-breath version, the smallest form of a practice, tiny enough to do even on the hardest day. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one breath counts. On a bad day, the smallest versions are plenty. That's day one hundred fifty-four.
